description: Mid-level engineer (3 to 5 years professional experience). Evaluates autonomous delivery, trade-off reasoning, subsystem architecture, observability, fault tolerance, and cross-functional collaboration without requiring constant supervision.

axes.depth: Thorough understanding of distributed patterns, database indexing, caching strategies, asynchronous processing, and system failure modes.
axes.ambiguity: Substantial ambiguity; candidate is expected to ask clarifying questions, establish boundary constraints, and justify non-functional trade-offs.
axes.expectedScope: Multi-component or service-level architecture, data pipeline, performance bottleneck resolution, and feature lifecycle from design to release.
axes.followUpPressure: Rigorous follow-ups examining edge cases under load, data inconsistency, migration strategies, and degradation policies.
axes.behavioralExpectations: Demonstrates strong ownership, ability to resolve moderate conflict with peers, mentoring junior developers, and delivering on commitments.

relevance.name: Relevance & Directness
relevance.description: Frames solutions around operational realities, SLA constraints, and tangible business/engineering requirements.

anchors.1: Gives purely academic definitions rather than evaluating real engineering trade-offs suitable for production systems.
anchors.3: Focuses directly on engineering trade-offs, service requirements, and concrete implementation choices.
anchors.5: Pinpoints the core architectural tension immediately; addresses latency, throughput, consistency, and operational complexity directly.

structure.name: Structural Framing
structure.description: Applies a structured architectural and behavioral methodology (e.g., Requirements -> Data Flow -> Trade-offs -> Bottlenecks).

anchors.1: Ad-hoc design that changes direction repeatedly without a clear guiding architecture or structured STAR story.
anchors.3: Well-organized presentation: outlines requirements, proposes a primary architecture, and discusses operational trade-offs.
anchors.5: Masterful presentation: systematically addresses functional and non-functional requirements, evaluates alternative designs, and synthesizes choices.

depth.name: Technical & Conceptual Depth
depth.description: Deep understanding of operational failure modes, concurrency, database indices, and system metrics.

anchors.1: Superficial knowledge; cannot explain how indexes work under the hood, how caches invalidate, or how connection pools behave.
anchors.3: Solid technical depth: explains cache invalidation, database isolation levels, message queues, and backpressure mechanisms.
anchors.5: Impressive technical depth: discusses p99 latency spikes, lock contention, write-amplification, and zero-downtime schema migrations.

clarity.name: Clarity & Articulation
clarity.description: Balances technical depth with clear, succinct summaries that keep the interviewer engaged.

anchors.1: Verbose, rambling answers that get lost in low-level trivia while missing high-level architectural clarity.
anchors.3: Speaks with clarity, confidence, and appropriate pacing; transitions cleanly between architectural concepts.
anchors.5: Highly articulate and engaging; uses vivid mental models, summarizes key trade-offs compactly, and invites active dialogue.

levelFit.name: Level Alignment
levelFit.description: Calibrated against autonomous 3-5 year engineer expectations for trade-off evaluation and system resilience.

anchors.1: Requires continuous hand-holding on standard design trade-offs or shows passive, reactive ownership.
anchors.3: Quintessential mid-level engineer: works autonomously, makes sound technical decisions, and understands production ramifications.
anchors.5: Exhibits senior-level instincts: proactively identifies hidden systemic risks, cost implications, and operational overhead.
